title: Palindromic Substrings — count all (expand-around-center).
shortTitle: Palindromic Substrings — Count All (Expand Around Center)

s1_definition.profdef: The Palindromic Substrings problem counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately even when the text is identical. The expand-around-center solution treats every character and every gap as a center and counts one palindrome for each successful expansion step outward while the mirrored characters match. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to count every symmetric segment inside a reference string, where the same segment at different places counts each time. Standing at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, each time you push outward and the two sides still match, that is one more palindrome to tally. You add up all these successful expansions across all centers.
s1_definition.oneliner: For every center, each outward step where both sides match is one more palindrome; sum them all.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Palindromic Substrings problem counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately even when the text is identical. The expand-around-center solution treats every character and every gap as a center and counts one palindrome for each successful expansion step outward while the mirrored characters match. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to count every symmetric segment inside a reference string, where the same segment at different places counts each time. Standing at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, each time you push outward and the two sides still match, that is one more palindrome to tally. You add up all these successful expansions across all centers.

**One line to remember:** For every center, each outward step where both sides match is one more palindrome; sum them all.

sections.s2_technical:
This is the counting cousin of the longest-palindrome problem, and it uses the same expand-around-center machinery. The difference is that instead of tracking the single longest span, you count how many palindromes each center yields. Every center yields at least one palindrome, the single character or, for even centers, requires the two adjacent characters to match to count even the smallest one.

For each of the two times n minus one centers, you expand outward. Each time the left and right characters are equal and both in bounds, you increment a running count, because the substring from left to right is itself a palindrome, then you move left back and right forward to check the next larger palindrome sharing that center. The moment the characters differ or you go out of bounds, you stop expanding this center and move to the next. The total count accumulates every palindrome centered anywhere.

The reason this counts correctly without double counting is that each palindrome has a unique center and a unique radius, so it is produced by exactly one center at exactly one expansion step. An odd-length palindrome comes from a character center, an even-length one from a gap center, and the expansion radius pins down its exact span. So summing one per successful expansion over all centers counts each distinct palindromic substring exactly once by position.

A senior point is the shared helper design. A single helper takes a left and right start, expands while the characters match, and returns the number of palindromes found from that center, which is simply the number of successful expansion steps. You call it with left equal to right for odd centers and left, right equal to i and i plus one for even centers, and sum the two returns across all i. This mirrors the longest-palindrome helper but returns a count instead of a length, which keeps the code clean and reuses the same reasoning.

Another senior point is the quadratic bound and the linear alternative. The worst case, a string of all identical characters, has a quadratic number of palindromic substrings, so even just enumerating them is quadratic and no algorithm can count them faster than producing them if it listed them; but counting only, Manacher's algorithm computes the per-center radii in linear time and sums them, giving linear total time for the count. I lead with expand-around-center for clarity and mention Manacher's as the linear option.

A small finance-domain example: `int count=0; for(int i=0;i<n;i++){ count+=expand(s,i,i); count+=expand(s,i,i+1); }` where expand returns the number of matching outward steps, totals all palindromic substrings.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India measures the structural symmetry of reference strings by counting how many palindromic segments they contain, as a feature in a pattern-scoring utility where more symmetric substrings suggest a more structured, possibly machine-generated identifier. The strings are moderate length, so a quadratic scan is fine. Counting palindromic substrings by expand-around-center is exactly this.

This is exactly how counting palindromic substrings works in Java — expanding around every center and tallying one palindrome per successful outward step.

Problem 2 — Single characters always count as palindromes, so a length-n string has at least n of them, and an empty string has zero, both of which the same code must produce. This shows the baseline single-character count and the empty-input edge case.

What the code will do: a `PalindromeCounter` with `countPalindromes(String s)` using expand-around-center over both parities with a counting helper. The demo counts palindromic substrings in several reference strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the reference string `aaa`.

Step 1: at index zero, the odd center expands: left and right both zero, `a` equals itself, count one for the single `a`, then left goes out of bounds and stops. The even center with left zero and right one compares `a` and `a`, match, count one for the substring `aa` spanning indices zero and one, then left out of bounds stops. So index zero contributed two palindromes.

Step 2: at index one, the odd center expands: `a` at one alone, count one, then left zero `a` and right two `a` match, count one for `aaa`, then out of bounds stops. So the odd center at index one contributed two, the single `a` and the full `aaa`.

Step 3: at index one, the even center with left one and right two compares `a` and `a`, match, count one for the substring `aa` spanning indices one and two, then left zero `a` and right three out of bounds stops. So index one contributed three total.

Step 4: at index two, the odd center gives the single `a`, count one, then out of bounds. The even center with left two and right three is out of bounds immediately, count zero. So index two contributed one.

Step 5: summing the contributions, index zero gave two, index one gave three, index two gave one, totaling six palindromic substrings: three single characters, two `aa` segments at different positions, and one `aaa`. For `abc`, each character is a palindrome but no two adjacent characters match, so the count is three.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Palindromic substrings = 3
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Count = 3
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Palindromic substrings = 6
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Count = 6
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "aaa"
    │ for each center i: expand odd (i,i) and even (i,i+1), count steps
    ▼
  i0 odd→1 (a) ; even→1 (aa)
  i1 odd→2 (a, aaa) ; even→1 (aa)
  i2 odd→1 (a) ; even→0
    │ sum = 1+1+2+1+1+0
    ▼
  count = 6
    ▼
  Output: total palindromic substrings
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Palindromic Substrings counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately, and I solve it with the same expand-around-center machinery as the longest-palindrome problem, in quadratic time and constant space. The difference is that instead of tracking the single longest span, I count one palindrome for every successful outward expansion step at every center.

For each of the two times n minus one centers, I expand outward while the mirrored characters match, incrementing the count each time they do, because the substring from the current left to right is itself a palindrome. A single helper returns the number of matching expansion steps from a given center, and I call it once for the odd center on each character and once for the even center in each gap, summing the results.

The reason this counts each palindrome exactly once, with no double counting, is that every palindromic substring has a unique center and a unique radius, so it is produced by exactly one center at exactly one expansion step. I also know the complexity floor: a string of all identical characters has a quadratic number of palindromic substrings, and while listing them is inherently quadratic, counting only can be done in linear time with Manacher's per-center radii, which I offer as the optimization while leading with the clearer expand-around-center.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a pattern-scoring utility that counts the palindromic segments in reference strings, where more symmetric substrings suggest a more structured, possibly machine-generated identifier worth flagging. Explaining the count-per-expansion idea, the unique-center-and-radius argument that prevents double counting, and the linear Manacher's alternative shows the interviewer that I understand both the mechanics and why the counting is correct.
